config.title: Test useFetch

intro.title: Test useFetch
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll learn how to test a custom Vue composable called `useFetch` that handles API data fetching. You'll build a test suite to verify that the composable correctly manages loading states, error handling, and data retrieval from an external API. The core concept involves using Vue's testing utilities to simulate API responses and assert expected behaviors. You'll work with Jest, Vue Test Utils, and mocking techniques to isolate your tests from real network calls. By the end, you'll understand how to write reliable tests for reactive composables in Vue applications.
intro.usecase: Testing custom hooks like useFetch is essential for building reliable data-driven applications. In real products, this pattern appears when developers need to ensure that API integrations in dashboards, admin panels, or e-commerce product listings work correctly under various conditions. For example, testing useFetch helps verify that a user's profile page loads their data without errors, or that a search filter fetches and displays updated results properly. This practice ensures that your application handles loading states, errors, and data updates consistently, leading to a more stable user experience.

objectives: Implement a test suite for the useFetch composable using Vue Test Utils
Configure mock responses for different HTTP status codes in useFetch tests
Manipulate component state to simulate loading and error scenarios
Construct assertions that verify data fetching behavior and error handling
Integrate test utilities to simulate user interactions with fetched data
Initialize test environments with proper mocks for network requests
Apply testing patterns to validate reactive updates from useFetch

steps.title: Import Vue and useFetch from vue

steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both Vue and useFetch from the vue module.

// Example: importing from a module

successCriteria: Vue and useFetch are imported from 'vue'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both Vue and useFetch from the 'vue' package. Check that your import statement includes both.

steps.seedCode:

// Create your TestUseFetch component here
</script>

<template>
  <!-- Component template will go here -->
</template>
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a basic Vue component structure with script and template sections ready for the next steps.
successCriteria: A Vue component named 'TestUseFetch' is created with both script and template sections
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both the script section (with component definition) and template section. The component should be named 'TestUseFetch'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember that Vue single-file components need both a <script> section for JavaScript logic and a <template> section for HTML structure. Create a component named 'TestUseFetch'.

const { data } = useFetch('https://api.example.com/data')

const { name, age, city } = getUserInfo();

steps.title: Add an error state display
steps.instruction: In your template, add a conditional paragraph element that displays the error message when the error state exists.
steps.hint: Use v-if to conditionally render an element based on the error state. Display the error message inside the paragraph.
steps.analogousExample:
// Conditional error display in Vue

{{ error.message }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will have a paragraph that shows the error message when the fetch fails.
successCriteria: A paragraph element with v-if="error" is added to the template, displaying the error message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using v-if with the error state and displaying the error message inside the paragraph.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error display isn't quite right. Check that you're using v-if with the error state and showing the error message.

steps.title: Display the fetched data
steps.instruction: In the template, add a paragraph element that displays the fetched data when it's available (when pending is false and error is false). Use the data object's properties like 'title' from the API response.
steps.hint: You can use v-else-if or v-else after the loading and error conditions to show the data. Access data properties with dot notation like data.title.
steps.analogousExample:
// Display data when available

{{ data.title }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show the fetched data (like a todo title) when the API call succeeds.
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added to display data properties (e.g., data.title) when pending and error are false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an element, but make sure it shows data properties (like data.title) and appears only when loading and error are false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The data display isn't set up correctly. Add a paragraph that shows data properties when the fetch is successful.

steps.title: Add a button to cancel the fetch
steps.instruction: Add a button element in your template with a click handler that calls the abort function from useFetch. The button should be labeled 'Cancel Fetch'.
steps.hint: The useFetch hook returns an abort function in its response. You can call it to cancel an ongoing request.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: adding a cancel button
<button @click="abort">Cancel Request</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'Cancel Fetch' button appears in the UI that can abort the ongoing fetch request when clicked.
successCriteria: A button element with @click="abort" and text 'Cancel Fetch' is added to the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the button has @click="abort" and the text 'Cancel Fetch'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or doesn't have the correct click handler. Check that you're calling the abort function from useFetch.

steps.title: Test the component functionality
steps.instruction: Run your Vue app in the browser and test all the useFetch features: verify the loading message appears, check that data displays correctly, test the refetch button, and try the cancel button.
steps.hint: Open your browser's developer tools to see network requests and console logs. You should see the loading message briefly, then the fetched todo data, and be able to trigger new requests or cancel ongoing ones.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your app should be fully functional with loading states, error handling, data display, and working refetch/cancel buttons.
successCriteria: All useFetch features work correctly: loading message appears during fetch, data displays when loaded, refetch button triggers new request, cancel button stops ongoing request.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Some features work but others need checking. Make sure all buttons trigger their intended actions and states update correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't functioning properly. Check that you've implemented all template elements and that useFetch is correctly configured.
